questions.q: Why can CPU-based autoscaling fail to trigger for a GPU inference workload that is genuinely overloaded?
options: Because autoscaling cannot be configured for GPU instances at all
Because CPU can sit near-idle while the GPU is pegged at 100% doing the actual model computation
Because GPU instances never report CPU metrics
Because CPU-based scaling only works below 1000 requests per second
questions.explain: The bottleneck is the GPU, not the CPU -- so a CPU threshold never crosses even when the service is saturated.

questions.q: What does the 'min instances' setting protect against, per this lesson?
options: A runaway bill from unconstrained scaling
Database schema incompatibility during a release
GPU driver version mismatches between instances
Cold starts and total unavailability by keeping a floor of running instances
questions.explain: Min instances is the floor -- it keeps at least that many instances running so requests don't all pay a cold-start penalty.

questions.q: What does the 'max instances' setting protect against?
options: Cold starts during low-traffic periods
Model checkpoint mismatches between instances
Your budget and GPU quota from a runaway traffic spike or a bug
Slow image builds during CI/CD
questions.explain: Max instances caps scaling so a traffic spike or bug doesn't translate into an unconstrained bill or exceed a GPU quota.

questions.q: Per this lesson, why does a GPU-backed inference instance typically take longer to start than a typical web service instance?
options: A bigger image, model weights loading into GPU memory, and GPU driver initialization
GPU instances must always be manually approved by an administrator
GPU instances require a full operating system reinstall on every start
Autoscaling is disabled by default for GPU instances
questions.explain: The lesson lists these specific reasons a GPU-backed instance starts in minutes rather than seconds.

questions.q: Because GPU-backed instances start slower, how does this lesson say AI autoscaling policies usually behave differently from typical web-service autoscaling?
options: They ignore traffic entirely and always run a fixed instance count
They scale in bigger, less frequent steps and lean more on the min floor to absorb short bursts
They scale a new instance for every single incoming request
They disable max instances entirely to avoid ever running out of capacity
questions.explain: Because starting a GPU instance is slow and often pricier, AI autoscaling leans on the min floor for bursts rather than reacting instance-by-instance to every fluctuation.
